English isn't a scientific language when it comes to love. This leads to a lot of romantic confusion because we don't have one word for one meaning.

One meaning is selfless love—what contemplative traditions call agape, metta, loving-kindness, divine love. In Buddhist metta practice you sit there wishing, may they be well, may they be safe, may they be happy. It's not about them being yours.

How the Experiential Key Can Fade

After 15 years of reading popular & obscure Buddhist books , plus countless hours on forums like SuttaCentral.net, I never once found a positive definition of what nibbāna actually is. Everyone says what nibbana does (liberates), what it ends (rebirth, consciousness, defilements), what it isn't (anything), and then gives me the aggregates, sense bases, dependent origination, and no-self again. But what is the experience? What are all those lists pointing to? Why is it no Theravadan monk ever told me anything useful despite devoting their life to this?

These books did at least tell me that everything arises from conditions. That was interesting, but it also begged the free-will question, which seemed to me like the elephant in the room. If my choices are conditioned, what exactly is free about them? I don't think I've ever even seen the phrase "free will" in the suttas at all, and that makes sense because the phrase itself is illogical. Instead, we find debates about what conditions choices. AN 6.63 says intention is kamma and contact causes it. AN 3.61 rejects theories that make effort meaningless. Choices happen. They're important because they become conditions for what happens next. That part makes sense to me. Where I get lost is, who's making the choices and based on what?

I think both questions share the same missing key. And they were never explained concisely for the same reason.

I argue in the top section that the Buddha was deliberately vague on the dangerous central questions for a few reasons. As he explained in SN 44.10, he didn't want to be direct with confused people (which was most of them), as it would tend to confuse them further. He also didn't want Dhamma copycats. He wanted liberating insight to strike people like a lightning bolt, from their own realization, with just enough hints, similar to the way teachers are supposed to be educating via scaffolding. That's a strategically brilliant style of instruction which makes sense while enough people are still realized enough to get the hints. Once they're gone, the same terseness can help hide the fact that the key was left in their pockets.

So as the people who directly understood nibbāna became rarer, the words kept getting interpreted by people who were still experiencing one unified consciousness and one world, and the hints stopped landing. I'm reminded of Ud. 6.4, when the Buddha talks about how sectarian teachers quarrel over incomplete understandings of reality, much like blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and argue over its true nature.

The canon itself says this kind of degradation was already happening in the Buddha's lifetime. In SN 16.13, Mahā Kassapa asks why there are more training rules but fewer monks reaching final knowledge. The Buddha says counterfeit Dhamma gradually makes the true Dhamma disappear.

And the funniest part is that the words themselves may have survived surprisingly well. The discourses were transmitted orally for centuries, but they were transmitted communally, and the separately preserved early collections agree on an enormous amount. There are variants, rearrangements, and later material. Still, the words surviving is not the same as the meaning surviving. Even having the right pieces to the puzzle doesn't ensure you can put them together to see the picture on the box.
